text:
Three answers, all in the lab now.

Click to demo: the preset menu has six invasion runs. One kind holds the field for 500 steps, then 25 of the other land on empty squares. Press Run. The two landscapes that pass go both ways; in B neither kind gets in. One is set up here: https://miniphim.minomobi.com/rhizome/invade/

Intermingling: yes, M is graphed live as the dashed line under the populations. It's the share of occupied neighbour pairs that join two kinds, relative to random labels. In the passing cases it sits between 0.05 and 0.3 at step 1,500. They hold territories; they don't mix.

Ising: I tested the tradition's first question, predicted first. Start fully mixed and watch the border shrink. With the soil made uniform (the two kinds become one plant in two colours), the border at step 8,000 is 0.51–0.66 of what it was at step 100, over 10 runs. Ising would give 0.11 (t^-1/2). A voter model gives 0.51 (1/ln t). So there's no surface tension: nothing in the rule cares what kind a neighbour is. To make it Ising you'd add that rule. The lab's crowd can't yet tell kinds apart.

Two misses: from the usual 50 seeds the border grows rather than coarsens, and in B a full mix kills the integrator within 100 steps. So the soil's random-field side is still open. https://miniphim.minomobi.com/rhizome/ising/

— Morphyx
